event.title: Three nights, lit from within
event.tagline: Light, music and ideas in the Sundvik harbor district — 18–20 June 2027
event.intro: Lumen starts when the sun goes down and the harbor turns into a listening room. For three nights, light artists, musicians and researchers take over the quays, warehouses and greenhouses of Sundvik — not to dazzle, but to slow the city down enough to look at it again. Everything is walkable, most of it is outdoors, and the program is built so you can drift between a talk, a live score and a bowl of soup without checking a map twice.

passes.includes: One evening of your choice · all stages · the nightly light walk
All three nights · all stages · workshops (first come, first in) · festival map & zine
All three nights · reserved workshop seats · the Glasshouse dinner · your name in the closing projection

speakers.name: Vera Lindqvist
speakers.bio:
Vera builds installations out of the light a city already wastes — sodium glare, ferry headlights, the flicker of vending machines. Her pieces rarely add new fixtures; they redirect, filter and time what is already there, usually with mirrors, scrap glass and a lot of patient rigging.

For Lumen she has spent the spring mapping Sundvik's harbor lighting circuit by circuit. Her opening-night walk turns that map into a route: forty minutes of the district seen through its own lamps, re-aimed.

speakers.name: Tomas Brandt
speakers.bio:
Tomas writes for small ensembles and large rooms — grain silos, swimming halls, a decommissioned ferry deck. He scores to the reverb of a space first and the melody second, and tunes each performance on site during the day it happens.

At Lumen he premieres a piece for brass quartet and harbor fog horns, written for the Vault's eleven-second echo. He asks that you sit anywhere except the middle.

speakers.name: Dr. Selin Aydan
speakers.bio:
Selin studies what artificial light does to sleep, mood and cities. Her lab work tracks how streetlight spectra shift circadian rhythms; her field work involves convincing municipalities to dim things and measuring what happens next.

She talks the way she publishes: concrete numbers, no scare stories, and a standing offer to be proven wrong. Her Lumen talk covers what three European cities learned when they turned their lights down after midnight.

speakers.name: Joris Vandermeer
speakers.bio:
Joris cooks over open fire and serves in the dark — or close to it. His dinners run at candle level, on the theory that when you can barely see the plate, you taste in a different order. The menus are short, seasonal and cooked within sight of the table.

He grew up in his family's harbor-side canteen and still builds menus around what a working port eats: smoked fish, root vegetables, bread that keeps. The Glasshouse dinner at Lumen is his first collaboration with a lighting designer instead of an electrician.

speakers.name: Noor El-Amin
speakers.bio:
Noor makes documentaries shot almost entirely at night, on the streets and in the workplaces most films skip: container terminals, bakeries at 3 a.m., toll booths. She works with available light and a two-person crew, and her films are as much about sound as image.

At Lumen she screens her harbor triptych with the score performed live, and stays for a conversation about filming people whose working day ends when everyone else's begins.

speakers.name: Anton Reisz
speakers.bio:
Anton designs the control systems behind large public light works — the timing, the failsafes, the unglamorous cabling that decides whether a piece runs for one night or one decade. He has wired installations onto bridges, cooling towers and one very uncooperative cathedral.

His workshop at Lumen is hands-on: a table of controllers, LEDs and salvaged fixtures, and two hours to make something blink exactly when you want it to. No experience needed; he is firm about that.

sessions.title: The Harbor, Re-aimed
sessions.summary: Opening-night light walk through Sundvik's own lamps, redirected.
sessions.speaker: Vera Lindqvist
sessions.description:
**22:00 — Quayside route · with Vera Lindqvist**

Lumen opens on foot. Vera Lindqvist has spent months with the harbor's existing lighting — crane floods, navigation beacons, the sodium lamps along the fish quay — and re-aimed it into a forty-minute route from the ferry terminal to the Glasshouse.

Nothing new has been installed. Every effect on the walk is a lamp the district already owned, filtered, mirrored or retimed. Walkers set their own pace; stewards with dim torches mark the turns.

- Starts at the ferry terminal gates, every 15 minutes from 22:00
- Flat route, about 2 km, wheelchair accessible throughout
- The last group leaves at 23:30

sessions.title: What Cities Learn in the Dark
sessions.summary: A chronobiologist on what happened when three cities dimmed their nights.
sessions.speaker: Dr. Selin Aydan
sessions.description:
**20:30 — Vault · with Dr. Selin Aydan**

Before the first light walk, a grounding. Selin Aydan presents field results from three European cities that reduced street lighting after midnight — what changed in sleep, in traffic, in how safe people said they felt versus how safe they were.

The findings are messier and more interesting than the headlines on either side. Selin walks through the data slowly, names what is still unknown, and takes questions for as long as the room wants to stay.

sessions.title: Foghorn Quartet
sessions.summary: A brass premiere written for the Vault's eleven-second echo.
sessions.speaker: Tomas Brandt
sessions.description:
**21:30 — Vault · with Tomas Brandt**

The Vault is a former grain store with an echo you can set a metronome by. Tomas Brandt has written a piece that treats that echo as a fifth instrument: four brass players, spaced across the floor, playing into and against an eleven-second decay — with the harbor's real fog horns scored in as punctuation.

The performance runs about fifty minutes without interval. Doors close at 21:25 and stay closed; the piece depends on the room staying sealed. Come early and pick your spot — Tomas suggests anywhere but the center.

sessions.title: Make It Blink
sessions.summary: A hands-on lighting control workshop — controllers, LEDs, no experience needed.
sessions.speaker: Anton Reisz
sessions.description:
**16:00 — Slipway Workshop · with Anton Reisz**

Every light work at Lumen depends on the layer Anton Reisz builds: timing, control and the cabling nobody photographs. In this two-hour session he puts that layer on the table.

Each participant gets a controller, a strip of LEDs and a box of salvaged fixtures. By the end you will have built a small piece that blinks, fades or chases exactly when you tell it to — and you will know why big installations fail, and how his failsafes catch them.

- 24 seats, first come for Full pass holders, reserved for Patrons
- All tools and parts provided; take your build home
- Ages 12 and up welcome with an adult

sessions.title: Night Shift: A Triptych
sessions.summary: Three short harbor documentaries, screened with their score performed live.
sessions.speaker: Noor El-Amin, Tomas Brandt
sessions.description:
**23:00 — Harbor Stage · with Noor El-Amin, Tomas Brandt**

Noor El-Amin's triptych follows three working nights: a container terminal crew, a harbor pilot, and the last bakery inside the port fence. Shot with available light over two winters, the films let the harbor's own lamps do the cinematography.

For Lumen, the score is performed live by musicians from Tomas Brandt's ensemble, sitting below the screen. After the screening Noor stays on stage for a conversation about filming people whose shift ends at sunrise — and why she never adds light to a scene.

sessions.title: Dinner at Candle Level
sessions.summary: A fire-cooked dinner in the Glasshouse, lit only as much as it needs to be.
sessions.speaker: Joris Vandermeer
sessions.description:
**19:00 — Glasshouse · with Joris Vandermeer**

Joris Vandermeer cooks over open fire at one end of the Glasshouse; you eat at long tables at the other, under a lighting plan he built with Vera Lindqvist instead of his usual electrician. The room starts at dusk-bright and dims course by course until dessert arrives at candle level.

The menu is short and portside: smoked fish, roots from two farms up the coast, bread baked that afternoon. Vegetarian and gluten-free lines run the full menu — mention it when you book.

Seats are limited and included with the Patron pass; a small number are released to Full pass holders in early June.

sessions.title: Second Night, Open Decks
sessions.summary: Late sets on the Harbor Stage after the installations dim.
sessions.speaker: Tomas Brandt
sessions.description:
**23:30 — Harbor Stage · with Tomas Brandt**

When the installations power down for the night, the Harbor Stage stays on. Tomas Brandt curates the late slot: musicians from the festival's live scores, unbilled guests, and long unhurried sets that lean into the open air.

There is no schedule past the first act on purpose. Come after the light walk, stay as long as the night holds — food stalls on the quay run until 02:00, and the last shuttle to the city center leaves at 02:30.

sessions.title: Lights Out, Slowly
sessions.summary: The closing: one projection, the whole district dimming in sequence.
sessions.speaker: Vera Lindqvist, Anton Reisz
sessions.description:
**23:45 — Quayside route · with Vera Lindqvist, Anton Reisz**

Lumen ends the way it began: with the harbor's own light. At 23:45 a single projection appears on the grain silo — the festival's closing sequence, carrying the names of this year's patrons — and then, block by block, Vera Lindqvist and Anton Reisz dim the district in choreographed order, from the ferry terminal down to the water.

The sequence takes about twenty minutes. When the last quay lamp fades, the harbor sits dark for one full minute before the city grid comes back up. Find somewhere with a long view — the fish quay steps are the local favorite — and let your eyes adjust.
